docs.text: Aeroboard Documentation ¶ Aeroboard is an Arrow-native telemetry platform for machine learning experiments. It combines a Python client, a Rust ingestion and history server, and a React dashboard so you can stream training metrics with low overhead and inspect them live or from persisted history. This documentation is organized for two audiences: Users who want to install Aeroboard, instrument training code, and inspect runs. Developers who want to understand the internals, extend storage backends, or contribute changes across the Python, Rust, and web components. What Aeroboard does ¶ Aeroboard focuses on a fast telemetry path: Python code buffers scalar metrics, hyperparameters, and images into Arrow RecordBatch payloads. Arrow Flight sends those batches to the Rust server. The Rust server fans batches out through a central broadcast hub. One path persists data through the configured storage engine. Another path serializes Arrow IPC frames to the dashboard over WebSockets. The result is a system that can support real-time updates without pushing chart rendering work back into your training process. Documentation map ¶ Getting started ¶ Installation covers prerequisites, environment setup, and the basic local workflow. Quickstart walks through bringing up the server, logging your first run, and querying the resulting data. User guide ¶ Core Concepts explains runs, auto-versioning, metric naming, buffering, and storage modes. Logging Data describes the Python SDK APIs for scalars, hyperparameters, images, and history queries. Framework Integrations covers the current PyTorch, Lightning, and Ray Tune patterns. Using the Dashboard explains how Aeroboard presents runs, summaries, comparisons, and image timelines. Developer guide ¶ Architecture explains the end-to-end runtime design. Repository Layout describes where code lives and which directory owns which concern. Development Workflow gives setup, test, lint, and local debugging guidance. Storage Model explains the storage abstraction and how filesystem, GreptimeDB, and live-only modes behave. Reference ¶ CLI lists the supported aeroboard commands. Python SDK documents the public client API. HTTP API documents the history and run-management endpoints. Configuration lists the current environment variables and runtime knobs. Typical local workflow ¶ For most contributors and users, the shortest path is: ./setup.sh uv run aeroboard start --storage filesystem uv run examples/torch_example.py Then open http://localhost:3000 and inspect the generated run. Build the docs locally ¶ Aeroboard uses MkDocs and is configured for hosting on Read the Docs. pip install -r docs/requirements.txt mkdocs serve To produce the static site: mkdocs build The generated output is written to site/ .

docs.text: Architecture ¶ This page describes the runtime architecture of Aeroboard as implemented today. High-level topology ¶ Aeroboard consists of three main runtime components and one optional persistence service: Python SDK for telemetry production. Rust server for ingestion, routing, persistence, and history APIs. React dashboard for visualization. GreptimeDB as an optional storage backend. Data path ¶ The core design goal is a low-copy telemetry path. Ingestion path ¶ The Python client buffers telemetry in process and periodically builds Arrow RecordBatch objects. It sends those batches to the Rust server over Arrow Flight. T-junction fan-out ¶ Inside the server, ingestion publishes batches into a tokio::sync::broadcast -based hub called TJunction . That hub splits traffic into two logical paths: persistence live streaming Persistence path ¶ The persistence loop subscribes to the same broadcast source and forwards supported telemetry into the configured StorageEngine implementation. Important property: live streaming should continue even if persistence fails. Live path ¶ WebSocket clients receive Arrow IPC-serialized batches from the same source. The frontend decodes those bytes with apache-arrow and merges them into typed-array stores. Server responsibilities ¶ The Rust server currently owns several concerns in one binary: Arrow Flight ingestion HTTP API endpoints WebSocket live streaming storage abstraction selection static frontend serving This is operationally simple for local use but deliberately centralizes a lot of responsibility into one process. Frontend data model ¶ The frontend avoids putting high-frequency series updates into React state. Instead, it maintains a store of typed arrays and only uses React for the surrounding view composition. That design matches the fact that timeseries updates are append-heavy and performance-sensitive. Current architectural strengths ¶ Arrow is used end to end across ingestion and live streaming. Arc<RecordBatch> keeps Rust-side clone costs low. The storage boundary is explicit in the server. Live updates are intentionally decoupled from persistence success. Current architectural constraints ¶ The server is still a single binary with several responsibilities. The Python client knows about run resolution through the HTTP API. Only a subset of possible telemetry shapes is supported end to end. The frontend expects certain history semantics regardless of storage mode, so empty but explicit responses matter. When you change the architecture ¶ If you add a new telemetry type, do not stop at one layer. You usually need coordinated changes in: Python schema and client buffering. Rust ingestion and telemetry-kind detection. Storage serialization and query support. HTTP response shaping if the UI reads it. Frontend decoding and rendering. The fastest way to create bugs in Aeroboard is to change only one half of the pipeline.

docs.text: Development Workflow ¶ This page covers the day-to-day workflow for contributing to Aeroboard. Initial setup ¶ The repository-standard bootstrap is: ./setup.sh That script uses uv for Python environment management and then builds both the frontend and the Rust server through the Aeroboard CLI. Running the system locally ¶ The main development entrypoint is: uv run aeroboard start --storage filesystem Use filesystem unless you are specifically working on Greptime-backed behavior. Recommended contributor loop ¶ For most changes: Start the server in filesystem mode. Run one of the example scripts or a focused local reproduction. Make code changes in the relevant component. Run targeted tests. Re-run the example or reproduction and verify dashboard behavior. Test commands ¶ Python tests ¶ uv run pytest Rust formatting ¶ cd aeroboard-server cargo fmt Web linting ¶ cd aeroboard-web npm run lint Working on storage backends ¶ When changing persistence, test at least these cases: filesystem mode live-only mode for empty-history semantics Greptime mode if your change touches the database-specific backend Storage regressions are easy to miss if you only validate one backend. Working on the Python client ¶ When changing the client API or batching logic: update examples if the public usage changed run the Python tests, especially payload and run-versioning coverage verify that flush() behavior still sends partial buffers at shutdown Working on the Rust server ¶ When changing server behavior: check the HTTP routes in main.rs verify query filtering and pagination semantics in history.rs keep live streaming resilient when persistence fails Working on the dashboard ¶ When changing frontend behavior: verify both initial history load and live updates pay attention to typed-array assumptions for scalar series test comparison and image timelines if your change affects history shape Documentation workflow ¶ The docs site is built with MkDocs. Preview locally: pip install -r docs/requirements.txt mkdocs serve Build the static site: mkdocs build Documentation changes should track real code behavior. If you update a command, endpoint, or public API, update the docs in the same change.

docs.text: Repository Layout ¶ This repository contains multiple language stacks in one workspace. Top-level directories ¶ aeroboard-client/ ¶ Python client package that exposes the telemetry SDK, CLI entrypoints, and integration helpers. Important paths: src/aeroboard_client/client.py : client implementation and framework integrations src/aeroboard_client/cli.py : top-level aeroboard CLI src/aeroboard_client/schema.py : Arrow schemas for supported telemetry types aeroboard-server/ ¶ Rust application that handles Flight ingestion, WebSocket live streaming, storage selection, and history APIs. Important paths: src/main.rs : application bootstrap and routing src/config.rs : runtime configuration from environment src/history.rs : HTTP handlers and history query shaping src/storage.rs : storage abstraction and backend implementations src/t_junction.rs : broadcast fan-out hub aeroboard-web/ ¶ React and Vite application for the dashboard. Important paths: src/hooks/useAeroboard.ts : main data ingestion and store logic src/components/ : UI widgets and plots examples/ ¶ Runnable example scripts for plain loops, Lightning, and Ray Tune. tests/ ¶ Python tests covering run versioning, payload generation, and client-level behavior. docs/ ¶ MkDocs source tree for this documentation site. Package layout notes ¶ The repository has both a top-level Python project configuration and a dedicated aeroboard-client package directory. When changing Python packaging or documentation, verify which path is authoritative for the behavior you are describing. Build outputs and generated artifacts ¶ Common generated output locations include: aeroboard-server/target/ for Rust build artifacts aeroboard-web/dist/ for the frontend bundle .aeroboard/ or custom data directories for filesystem persistence logs/ for captured example runs in this repository snapshot Do not document generated artifacts as if they are source-owned unless the workflow explicitly depends on them.

docs.text: Storage Model ¶ Aeroboard routes all persistence and history queries through the Rust StorageEngine trait. Why the storage abstraction matters ¶ The live telemetry path and the persistence path are intentionally separated. That design only stays clean if storage-specific behavior is isolated behind a narrow server-side interface. The storage engine currently exposes operations for: appending telemetry batches querying scalar history querying hyperparameters querying image history listing runs clearing history Supported storage modes ¶ Filesystem ¶ Filesystem storage is the default mode. The server writes run-scoped data under the configured data directory, currently defaulting to .aeroboard . Conceptually the layout looks like this: .aeroboard/ runs/ <encoded-run-id>/ manifest.json scalars/ <timestamp>-<uuid>.arrow hyperparameters/ <timestamp>-<uuid>.arrow images/ <encoded-metric-name>/ index.json <timestamp>-<uuid>.<format> Important details: a manifest is written per run so the run can be enumerated later scalar and hyperparameter data are stored as Arrow files images are extracted and stored as individual files plus an index Filesystem mode is usually the best place to validate new telemetry behavior because it keeps the persistence path transparent. GreptimeDB ¶ Greptime mode routes persistence and historical queries through the configured Greptime HTTP endpoint. Use it when you specifically want database-backed persistence or need to validate the Greptime-specific code path. Live-only ¶ Live-only mode intentionally accepts batches without persisting them. Expected semantics: ingestion succeeds live streaming still works history queries return empty collections delete-style persistence operations should not pretend they succeeded against nonexistent stored data Query semantics shared across backends ¶ The HTTP history layer applies consistent filters after retrieving rows from storage: run_id accepts a comma-separated list metric accepts a comma-separated list start_ms and end_ms are inclusive cursor and limit implement position-based pagination These semantics need to remain backend-agnostic. Adding a new storage backend ¶ If you add another storage engine: Implement the StorageEngine trait. Wire it into backend selection in build_storage . Preserve the empty-history contract where appropriate. Make sure list_runs() supports run resolution and UI enumeration. Verify that failures in persistence do not break the live path. Adding a new telemetry type ¶ A new telemetry type usually requires more than a storage change. Checklist: Add or extend the Arrow schema in the Python client. Teach ingestion to classify the new batch kind. Decide whether the storage engine persists it, streams it, or both. Extend query APIs if the frontend needs historical access. Add examples and tests. If you skip the query or storage contract, the UI may appear partially broken even when ingestion itself succeeds.

docs.text: Installation ¶ This page covers the local setup needed to run Aeroboard and build its documentation. Prerequisites ¶ Aeroboard spans Python, Rust, and a React frontend, so the full development setup needs tools from each stack. Required for the standard local workflow: uv for Python dependency management and command execution. Python 3.9 or newer. Node.js and npm for the dashboard build. Rust and cargo for the server build. Optional depending on the storage mode you use: Docker and Docker Compose for GreptimeDB. Full project setup ¶ The repository ships with a top-level setup script that installs Python dependencies through uv , builds the frontend bundle, and builds the Rust server. chmod +x setup.sh ./setup.sh That script performs these steps: uv sync --extra examples --dev uv run aeroboard setup npm install && npm run build inside aeroboard-web cargo build --release inside aeroboard-server Manual setup ¶ If you prefer to run the steps yourself: uv sync --extra examples --dev uv run aeroboard setup The CLI setup command will rebuild both the frontend and the Rust server. Running Aeroboard ¶ Start the HTTP server, WebSocket endpoint, and Arrow Flight ingestion server: uv run aeroboard start Default ports: HTTP dashboard and API: 3000 Arrow Flight ingestion: 50051 Useful variants: uv run aeroboard start --storage filesystem --data-dir .aeroboard uv run aeroboard start --storage greptime uv run aeroboard start --storage live uv run aeroboard start --port 3100 --flight-port 51051 Running GreptimeDB ¶ GreptimeDB is optional. Filesystem storage is the default and is usually the simplest local mode. If you want database-backed persistence: uv run aeroboard db uv run aeroboard start --storage greptime To stop the database: uv run aeroboard stop-db Installing optional client integrations ¶ Some integrations depend on optional extras: Ray Tune example: uv sync --extra ray --dev Lightning examples: included in the root project dependencies Verifying the installation ¶ The CLI includes a status check: uv run aeroboard status That command checks: The HTTP API on port 3000 The Flight endpoint on port 50051 The GreptimeDB health endpoint on port 4000 Documentation dependencies ¶ The docs site is built with MkDocs and is configured for Read the Docs hosting. pip install -r docs/requirements.txt mkdocs serve If you already use uv for everything, you can also run MkDocs through the environment you manage yourself after installing the dependency there.

docs.text: Quickstart ¶ This quickstart takes you from a clean checkout to a visible run in the dashboard. 1. Build the project ¶ ./setup.sh 2. Start the server ¶ Use filesystem storage first. It has the lowest operational overhead and matches the current default. uv run aeroboard start --storage filesystem --data-dir .aeroboard Once the server is running, open http://localhost:3000 . 3. Log a first run ¶ You can use one of the bundled examples: uv run examples/torch_example.py Or create a minimal script: import aeroboard_client as aeroboard client = aeroboard.init(run_id="quickstart-demo") client.log_hyperparameters({"optimizer": "adamw", "lr": 1e-3}) for step in range(10): client.log_metrics({"loss": 1.0 / (step + 1), "accuracy": step / 10}, step=step, prefix="train") client.flush() Run it with: uv run your_script.py 4. Inspect the dashboard ¶ After metrics start arriving, the dashboard will: Load persisted history from the HTTP API. Subscribe to the live telemetry stream over WebSocket. Render scalar metrics from typed-array stores. Show hyperparameters in comparison-oriented views. If you log images, they also appear in the timeline viewer. 5. Query history programmatically ¶ The Python client can query the HTTP API as well: import aeroboard_client as aeroboard client = aeroboard.init(run_id="quickstart-demo") history = client.query_history(metric="train/loss") print(history["rows"][:3]) 6. Understand run naming ¶ Run identifiers are auto-versioned. If quickstart-demo already exists, Aeroboard will resolve a new identifier such as quickstart-demo-v2 or quickstart-demo-v3 . Resolution happens by asking the server for /api/runs/resolve , with a fallback to listing runs from /api/runs if necessary. 7. Switch storage modes when needed ¶ Use these modes depending on what you need: filesystem : best default for local development and demos. greptime : database-backed persistence through GreptimeDB. live : no persistence, live streaming only. In live mode, the dashboard can still show new incoming data, but persisted history endpoints return empty results.

docs.text: HTTP API Reference ¶ Aeroboard serves an HTTP API from the same process that hosts the dashboard and WebSocket endpoint. Base URL by default: http://localhost:3000 GET /api/history ¶ Returns persisted scalar history plus aggregated run summaries. Query parameters ¶ Parameter Type Meaning run_id string Single run ID or comma-separated run IDs metric string Single metric name or comma-separated metric names start_ms integer Inclusive lower timestamp bound in milliseconds end_ms integer Inclusive upper timestamp bound in milliseconds limit integer Maximum number of rows to return cursor integer Position-based pagination cursor Response shape ¶ { "rows": [ { "ts_ms": 1740000000000, "run_id": "baseline", "name": "train/loss", "value": 0.42 } ], "run_summaries": [ { "run_id": "baseline", "hyperparameters": [ {"key": "lr", "value": "0.001", "value_type": "float"} ], "metric_summaries": [ {"name": "train/loss", "last": 0.42, "min": 0.42, "max": 1.1} ] } ], "next_cursor": null, "error": null } Notes ¶ filtering happens with OR semantics within comma-separated run_id or metric sets time bounds are inclusive pagination is position-based rather than opaque-token based the endpoint returns explicit empty arrays and an optional error string if storage fails DELETE /api/history ¶ Clears persisted history through the configured storage backend. Response shape ¶ { "deleted": true, "error": null } In live-only mode, deletion should not be treated as a normal persisted-history operation. GET /api/history/images ¶ Returns persisted image history. Query parameters ¶ Uses the same filter fields as GET /api/history : run_id metric start_ms end_ms limit cursor Response shape ¶ { "rows": [ { "ts_ms": 1740000000000, "run_id": "baseline", "name": "samples/prediction", "format": "png", "image_base64": "..." } ], "next_cursor": null, "error": null } GET /api/runs ¶ Lists known run IDs. Response shape ¶ { "runs": ["baseline", "baseline-v2"] } POST /api/runs/resolve ¶ Returns the canonical run ID that should be used for a proposed base run name. Request body ¶ { "base_run_id": "baseline" } Response shape ¶ { "run_id": "baseline-v2" } Versioning rules ¶ a brand new base name is returned unchanged if the base name already exists, the next highest version suffix is used framework suffixes such as -pl2.5.1 are preserved while versioning GET /ws/live ¶ Upgrades to a WebSocket connection and streams live Arrow IPC batches. The frontend uses this endpoint for real-time updates after loading persisted history.

Module-level helpers ¶ Import style: import aeroboard_client as aeroboard Available helpers: Function Purpose init(...) Create and register the default client get_default_client() Return the current default client or None log(metrics) Log scalar metrics through the default client log_metrics(metrics, step=None, prefix=None) Log metrics with optional prefixing and shared step log_hyperparameters(hyperparameters, step=None) Log hyperparameters log_image(name, image, format=None, timestamp_ms=None) Log an image flush() Flush the default client AeroboardClient ¶ Constructor: AeroboardClient( run_id=None, url="grpc://localhost:50051", batch_size=100, api_base_url=None, ) Core attributes ¶ Attribute Meaning base_run_id The requested run name before resolution run_id The resolved canonical run name url Flight endpoint api_base_url HTTP API base for run resolution and history queries batch_size Client-side buffer threshold Logging methods ¶ log(metrics: dict[str, float]) ¶ Logs raw scalar metrics. log_metrics(metrics, step=None, prefix=None) ¶ Convenience method for training loops. Rules: non-numeric values are skipped scalar tensors are coerced when possible prefix is only applied to names without / step is logged as the scalar metric step log_hyperparameters(hyperparameters, step=None) ¶ Stores hyperparameters as string values plus a value_type classification. log_image(name, image, format=None, timestamp_ms=None) ¶ Stores image payloads for timeline-style inspection. The client accepts multiple image input forms and normalizes them to encoded bytes before upload. Flush and lifecycle methods ¶ flush() ¶ Flushes scalar, hyperparameter, and image buffers to the Flight server. close() ¶ Flushes remaining buffers and closes the underlying Flight client. Query methods ¶ query_history(...) ¶ Returns a dictionary with: rows run_summaries next_cursor Accepted filters: run_id metric from_timestamp to_timestamp limit cursor query_hyperparameters(...) ¶ Returns a flattened list of hyperparameter entries extracted from history summaries. query_images(...) ¶ Returns image history rows from /api/history/images and can optionally filter by image format client-side. list_runs() ¶ Returns the server-reported run identifiers. Exceptions ¶ Exception Meaning AeroboardClientError Base client error for query or client-side failures FlightConnectionError Raised when ingestion is attempted without a working Flight connection Lightning integration ¶ lightning_logger(...) ¶ Preferred helper for Lightning projects. It is deprecated in favor of lightning_logger(...) . AeroboardLightningCallback ¶ Alternative callback-based integration for Lightning. Ray Tune integration ¶ AeroboardRayTuneLoggerCallback ¶ Creates one Aeroboard run per Ray trial, logs trial configuration as hyperparameters, and forwards numeric result values as scalar metrics. Arrow schemas ¶ The current public schemas are defined in aeroboard_client.schema . docs.text: Core Concepts ¶ This page explains the concepts that shape how Aeroboard behaves at runtime. Runs ¶ A run is the primary unit of organization in Aeroboard. Every metric point, hyperparameter entry, and image is associated with a run_id . Examples: baseline baseline-v2 lightning-eval-filesystem-baseline experiment-pl2.5.1 Auto-versioning ¶ The Python client does not blindly reuse a run name. When a client first needs its canonical run identifier, it asks the backend whether the requested base name already exists. If the name is already taken, Aeroboard chooses the next free version suffix: experiment -> experiment-v2 experiment-v2 and experiment-v4 already exist -> next becomes experiment-v5 Framework suffixes such as -pl2.5.1 are preserved when versioning Lightning-oriented names. Telemetry types ¶ Aeroboard currently supports three public telemetry categories from the Python SDK. Scalars ¶ Scalars are numeric values such as losses, accuracies, learning rates, epochs, and steps. The scalar Arrow schema is: Field Type timestamp timestamp[ms] run_id string name string value float64 Hyperparameters ¶ Hyperparameters are stored as stringified values plus a declared value type. The hyperparameter Arrow schema is: Field Type timestamp timestamp[ms] run_id string key string value string value_type string Images ¶ Images are stored as encoded bytes and accompanied by a declared format. The image Arrow schema is: Field Type timestamp timestamp[ms] run_id string name string image_data binary format string Metric naming ¶ Metric names are free-form strings, but some conventions matter: Metrics named step are treated specially by the frontend for alignment. Names ending in /step should also be treated as x-axis index metrics. Prefixing metrics with namespaces such as train/ , val/ , or optimizer/ makes the dashboard easier to read. The convenience API log_metrics(..., prefix="train") automatically prefixes bare names like loss to train/loss , while leaving already-qualified names such as optimizer/lr unchanged. Batching and flushing ¶ The Python client buffers telemetry in memory before sending Arrow batches through Flight. Scalars flush when the scalar buffer reaches batch_size . Hyperparameters flush when their buffer reaches batch_size . Images flush more aggressively, at roughly one quarter of the configured batch size. Call flush() explicitly at the end of a training run so partially filled buffers are sent. Storage modes ¶ Aeroboard supports three storage modes. Filesystem ¶ The server persists batches under a local data directory. This is the current default and is the simplest option for local use. GreptimeDB ¶ The server persists history to GreptimeDB and queries it back through HTTP APIs. Live-only ¶ The server keeps the live stream active but intentionally skips persistence. History queries return empty results rather than failing. Live stream versus history ¶ Aeroboard uses two complementary paths: A live path for low-latency dashboard updates over WebSocket. A history path for persisted queries over HTTP. This split is important operationally. A storage failure should not stop live streaming, and a live-only deployment should still behave predictably when the UI queries history.

docs.text: Using the Dashboard ¶ The dashboard is the browser-facing part of Aeroboard. It combines persisted history with the live telemetry stream so runs appear immediately while still remaining queryable after reload. How the dashboard gets data ¶ On startup, the frontend does two things: Fetches persisted history from the HTTP API. Opens a WebSocket to /ws/live for new batches. This split lets the UI recover existing data after a refresh and then continue updating in real time. What the dashboard shows ¶ The current UI is oriented around experiment inspection and comparison. Scalar charts ¶ Scalar metrics are decoded from Arrow IPC frames and stored in typed arrays before being rendered with uPlot . Practical implications: high-frequency metric streams remain cheap to render the UI benefits from metrics that include a shared step consistent metric names make comparison easier Run summaries ¶ The history API returns run_summaries alongside raw rows. Those summaries include: hyperparameters per run per-metric last value per-metric minimum per-metric maximum These summaries drive overview and comparison-oriented widgets. Comparison views ¶ Hyperparameters are especially useful in views that compare multiple runs side by side. If you want those views to be meaningful, log hyperparameters early in the run. Image timeline ¶ Images are shown as historized frames ordered by timestamp. This works best when you log the same image name repeatedly over time, for example: samples/prediction diagnostics/gradient-norms validation/input-preview Best practices for readable runs ¶ Use a clear run prefix such as baseline , ablation-dropout , or ray-search . Keep metric names stable across related runs. Always emit a step metric or use log_metrics(..., step=...) . Log hyperparameters before or early in training. Use consistent image names when logging timelines. Storage-mode implications ¶ The dashboard works differently depending on the server mode. Filesystem and Greptime modes ¶ Both support: persisted history reloads run listing comparison summaries image history queries Live-only mode ¶ Live-only mode supports: live updates over WebSocket It intentionally does not provide persisted history. The history endpoints return empty collections instead of historical data. Troubleshooting empty views ¶ If the dashboard is empty: Confirm the server is running. Confirm your client is pointing at the correct Flight and HTTP ports. Check whether you are in live mode and expecting persisted history. Make sure your script calls flush() before exiting. Use uv run aeroboard status to inspect what the local server can see.

docs.text: Framework Integrations ¶ Aeroboard is designed to work both with explicit training loops and with common ML framework hooks. Plain Python or PyTorch loops ¶ The simplest pattern is to keep an AeroboardClient instance alongside your optimizer and training loop. import aeroboard_client as aeroboard client = aeroboard.init(run_id="torch-demo", batch_size=50) client.log_hyperparameters({"optimizer": "adam", "lr": 1e-3}) for step in range(1000): client.log_metrics({"loss": loss, "accuracy": accuracy}, step=step, prefix="train") client.flush() This pattern gives you the most control over metric names and flush timing. PyTorch Lightning logger ¶ For Lightning, the preferred integration is lightning_logger() : import aeroboard_client as aeroboard import lightning.pytorch as pl client = aeroboard.init(run_id="lightning-demo") logger = client.lightning_logger() trainer = pl.Trainer(logger=logger) trainer.fit(model) The logger: forwards metrics emitted through LightningModule.log(...) records hyperparameters passed through Lightning's logger interface tracks the most recent step value and reuses it when Lightning omits an explicit step flushes remaining telemetry during save() and finalize() PyTorch Lightning callback ¶ Aeroboard also exposes AeroboardLightningCallback . Use it if you want a callback-oriented integration instead of a logger-oriented one. The callback attempts to: log model and logger hyperparameters at fit start emit training metrics at the end of train batches emit validation summaries at validation epoch end flush data when training ends The logger is the cleaner default when your training code already follows Lightning's logging model. Ray Tune callback ¶ Aeroboard ships with AeroboardRayTuneLoggerCallback , which creates one Aeroboard run per Ray trial. from ray import tune import aeroboard_client as aeroboard callback = aeroboard.AeroboardRayTuneLoggerCallback( run_prefix="ray-demo", metric_prefix="train", ) Behavior: each trial gets its own Aeroboard run trial configuration is logged as hyperparameters numeric trial results are streamed as scalar metrics standard Ray metadata such as trial identifiers is attached as hyperparameters Example workflows in this repository ¶ The repository includes runnable examples: examples/torch_example.py examples/lightning_example.py examples/ray_tune_example.py The Lightning example is especially useful for comparing filesystem and Greptime-backed runs because it tags each run with storage metadata that appears in comparison views. Choosing an integration style ¶ Use this rule of thumb: Prefer direct AeroboardClient calls in plain loops or when you need tight control. Prefer lightning_logger() for Lightning projects. Prefer AeroboardRayTuneLoggerCallback for Ray Tune experiments. When in doubt, start with direct client logging because it makes metric naming and flush behavior explicit.

docs.text: Logging Data ¶ This page focuses on the Python SDK that application code uses to emit telemetry and query history. Initialize a client ¶ The public entrypoint is the module-level init() helper: import aeroboard_client as aeroboard client = aeroboard.init( run_id="my-run", url="grpc://localhost:50051", api_base_url="http://localhost:3000", batch_size=100, ) Important parameters: run_id : base run name before auto-versioning. url : Arrow Flight endpoint. api_base_url : HTTP base URL used for run resolution and history queries. batch_size : client-side telemetry buffer size. The module also keeps a default client so helpers like aeroboard.log(...) can be used without passing the client object around. Log scalar metrics ¶ Use log() when you already have the exact metric payload you want to send: client.log({"train/loss": 0.42, "train/accuracy": 0.91, "step": 10}) Only numeric values are emitted. Non-numeric entries are ignored. Log metrics with prefixing and shared step ¶ Use log_metrics() for training-loop style code: client.log_metrics( {"loss": loss, "accuracy": accuracy, "optimizer/lr": current_lr}, step=global_step, prefix="train", ) Behavior: Bare names like loss become train/loss when prefix="train" is provided. Existing names with a slash are kept as-is. The provided step is added as a separate scalar metric named step . Scalar tensors are coerced to floats when possible. Log hyperparameters ¶ Use log_hyperparameters() for values you want to compare across runs: client.log_hyperparameters({ "optimizer": "adamw", "lr": 0.001, "dropout": 0.2, "batch_size": 64, }) Supported value categories include common scalar types, booleans, strings, and list-like values that can be stringified meaningfully. None values are ignored. The dashboard uses these entries in comparison-oriented views. Log images ¶ Use log_image() for snapshots you want to inspect over time: client.log_image("samples/prediction", image_bytes, format="png") Accepted input types include: Raw bytes PIL images NumPy arrays Torch tensors that can be converted into image data The client may recompress images to keep payload sizes manageable. Large images are constrained by an internal maximum payload budget. Query history ¶ The SDK also wraps the HTTP history API. Query scalar history ¶ response = client.query_history( run_id="my-run", metric="train/loss", from_timestamp=0, to_timestamp=9999999999, limit=200, ) rows = response["rows"] run_summaries = response["run_summaries"] next_cursor = response["next_cursor"] Query hyperparameters ¶ entries = client.query_hyperparameters(run_id="my-run") This currently works by reading the run summaries returned from the history endpoint. Query image history ¶ images = client.query_images(run_id="my-run", name="samples/prediction", limit=20) Returned image rows include base64-encoded image data and a declared format. List runs ¶ runs = client.list_runs() End-of-run cleanup ¶ Call flush() before your process exits: client.flush() client.close() close() also performs a final flush. Failure behavior ¶ If the Flight client cannot connect, ingestion methods raise FlightConnectionError . Query helpers raise AeroboardClientError when HTTP requests fail. This means instrumentation code should either ensure the server is already running or handle those exceptions explicitly when Aeroboard is optional in a workflow.
